en: Salutations to the speech of Śrī Gaṇeśa! I bow to the Lord of the Gaṇas, the son of Pārvatī, the destroyer of obstacles, who has a protruding belly, a massive body, long lips, and ears like those of an elephant.
No one other than a bearer of weapons can reach the further shore of the science of archery;
therefore, when night has fallen, one should contemplate the reality of Śiva in a dream.
Therefore, the mind should not be placed upon the swing of doubt regarding this work,
*Vīracintāmaṇi*, by those who are skilled in the art of poetry.
Through practice of which archers are perfected by grace and become conquerors of enemy armies— let that practice be undertaken.
Even if there is but one renowned archer in a city,
enemies flee far away from it, just as deer do from the presence of a lion.
The preceptor should bestow the bow upon a Brāhmaṇa who has been thoroughly examined;
it is not given to one who is deceitful, a rogue, ungrateful, or of dull intellect.
A bow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa, and a sword indeed to a Kṣatriya;
one should cause a spear to be given to a Vaiśya, and a mace to a Śūdra.
The bow, the discus, the spear, the sword, the dagger, the mace,
and seventhly, wrestling— thus are the seven types of combat.
The preceptor (Ācārya) shall be with seven warriors, Bhārgava likewise with four;
the combatant (Yoddhā) shall be with two, and the astrologer (Gaṇaka) shall be with one.
Hasta, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās,
Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Revatī, and likewise the tenth [nakṣatra], Mūla.
One should cause all rites to be performed when the moon is situated in the birth sign, or in the third, sixth, seventh, tenth, or eleventh house.
The third, fifth, seventh, ninth,
twelfth, and thirteenth lunar days are likewise considered auspicious.
Sunday, Friday, and likewise Thursday—
these three days are auspicious for the commencement of surgical procedures.
During these days, the preceptor should cause the weapons to be given to the disciple,
having gratified the gods with gifts and fire-offerings according to the scriptural injunctions.
One should feed the Brahmins there, as well as many young maidens;
one should worship with devotion the ascetics and others who are Śiva-yogins.
There, one should worship the guru with food, drink, and the like, as well as with garments, ornaments, decorations, and various fragrant garlands.
Having observed a fast and having joined his palms in reverence, the disciple,
with hands folded in añjali, should request the bow from the guru.
Then, the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) as taught by Śiva should be performed by the preceptor for the disciple who desires spiritual accomplishment; it destroys sin and eliminates obstacles.
One should place Īśa at the site of the crest-lock (śikhā), Keśava on the pair of arms,
Brahmā in the middle of the navel, and Gaṇādhipa on the two shanks.
This is the mantra for the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkara in the middle of the crest-lock. Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Keśava in the two arms.
Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Brahmā in the middle of the navel.
Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati in the two shanks.
One should cause such a ritual placement (nyāsa) to be performed by which there will be welfare;
furthermore, other wicked beings shall never cause harm.
To the disciple, one should give a human bow consecrated with the science of archery (dhanurveda), according to the Vedic injunctions, using the mantra "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt... and so forth.
First, one should perform the "flower-piercing" with a shaft devoid of a point;
thereafter, one should perform the "fish-piercing" with a shaft provided with a point.
Then one should perform the "flesh-piercing" (māṃsavedha); thus the piercing is threefold.
Arrows prepared by men with the aforementioned piercings shall be effective for all purposes.
Likewise, when the fall of the arrow occurs after drawing it back during the piercing,
one who relies upon the eastern quarter shall always be victorious and happy.
In the south, there will be terrible quarrels and, furthermore, departure to a foreign land;
in the west, wealth and grain; and in the north, everything indeed shall come to pass.
A fall in the northeast is inauspicious; other intermediate directions are auspicious, as they bring about all nourishment and grant success in the performance of surgical operations.
Having thus performed the three piercings amidst the sounds of conchs and drums,
he should then bow to the guru and present the bow and arrows.
The first bow should be of human proportions, and the second a war-bow;
it should be auspicious, slightly less than the measure of the strength of one's own arms.
An archer who excels his own life-force is better than a bow that exceeds his life-force;
for an archer oppressed by his bow cannot see his target.
Therefore, a bow that measures one's own strength will bring about auspicious results;
the bow of the gods is the best, and that of humans is inferior to it.
A bow measuring five and a half cubits is proclaimed to be the best;
that should be known as the divine bow held by Śaṅkara in ancient times.
Therefore, it was received from Paraśurāma by the wise Droṇa;
from Droṇa it was taken by Pārtha, and from him it was held by Sātyaki.
In the Kṛta age, Mahādeva; in the Tretā age, Bhārgava;
and in the Dvāpara age, the brahmin Droṇa held the divine bow.
A cubit (hasta) consists of twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgula), and a bow (dhanus) consists of four cubits;
that shall be the human bow, endowed with all the proper characteristics.
The bow is proclaimed to have three joints, five joints, seven joints, and nine joints;
these four types bestow auspiciousness.
One should avoid bows with four joints, six joints, or eight joints;
for some, however, the bow may measure nine spans (vitasti).
One should not perform [the rite] with wood that is excessively old, unseasoned, or handled by a relative; nor with wood that is burnt, split, or has been grasped by an outsider or an insider.
The wise should never perform a *galagranthi* or *talagranthi* on one who is devoid of good qualities, one who is burdened by vices, or one who is afflicted by the defects of the *kāṇḍa*.
If uncooked, it leads to fracture; if over-ripe, it becomes harsh. When one is insolent toward kinsmen, there arises agitation and quarreling with relatives.
When a house is burned by fire, it is destroyed along with its openings; likewise, when the intellect is destroyed, the external object of perception cannot be found, nor can it be found within.
But when an arrow is aimed at an inferior target, it causes a rout in battle;
however, once the target has been overtaken, the firm mark is no longer reached.
A goiter, a knot on the sole of the foot, and a bow-shaped curvature cause the loss of wealth;
free from these defects, [the body] brings about all auspicious characteristics.
The divine bow Śārṅga, however, is the supreme weapon of Viṣṇu;
it was fashioned by Viśvakarman with a measurement of seven vitastis.
Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor upon earth, was that bow in the possession of anyone;
it could not be brought under control by anyone, except for the one Supreme Person.
But that which is a human-made work, constructed with great effort and measured by seven spans (vitastis), accomplishes all purposes.
Generally, the Śārṅga bow is known as the weapon for elephant-riders;
for chariot-warriors and foot-soldiers, the bamboo bow (vāṃśa-cāpa) is proclaimed.
I shall describe the characteristics of the bowstring and how the string should be made:
it should be three times the length of the bow, seamless, and fashioned from triple-stranded threads.
The cord should be spun fine, capable of withstanding all tasks in battle;
the cord should be made of silk threads, equal in measure to the little finger.
In the absence of silk thread, the sinew of a deer is desired;
furthermore, for the sake of its strength, the sinews of buffaloes or cows may be taken.
At that time, one should make an excellent cord from the skin of a slain cow-eared deer or a goat,
in the form of single-stranded woolen threads.
The cord should be made from the bark of a mature bamboo cane; it must be old and firm, bound with silk thread, and capable of enduring all tasks in battle.
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, the bark of the Arka tree is praised;
its quality there should be made into a sacred, stationary, and firm [seat].
The cubits for the threads of the circular sun-line are recorded as eighteen;
that circle should be made threefold, and this is the measurement of the cord.
As for the blade of pure iron, it should be provided with a handle and a sharp point;
one should join it with a diamond-paste (vajralepa) according to the requirements of its core and wings.
The arrow with a broad head, the razor-edged arrow, the cow-tail shaped, the crescent-shaped,
the needle-mouthed, the bhalla, the calf-tooth shaped, and the very beloved [vatsadanta].
The *karṇika* and *kākatuṇḍa*, as well as many others,
exist in various regions as fruits of manifold forms.
With the arrow-head shaped like a plowshare, he struck the shield; with the razor-edged arrow, the bow; with the needle-headed arrow, the armor; and with the crescent-headed arrow, the head.
The heart is to be pierced with a *bhallā* arrow, and likewise with two *bhallas*;
iron is to be pierced with a *kākatuṇḍa*, and the target with a *gopucchaka*.
The other, known as the gopucchaka, should be understood as being fashioned from pure bell-metal;
its diameter at the mouth and at the neck is measured by one finger-breadth.
I shall describe the administration of the fruit and the application of divine herbs,
by which one may pierce even impenetrable armor as easily as a tree leaf.
One should grind long pepper, rock salt, and costus with cow's urine;
with this one should smear the surgical instrument and, once smeared, heat it over a fire.
When the medicinal substance has been cast into the fire without spilling and thoroughly stirred with force,
and the iron has subsequently been quenched therein, it excels in this process of piercing.
One should smear the blade with these five salts ground together with honey, beeswax, and mustard seeds; once smeared, one should heat it in fire.
One should know that the supreme medicinal blade, which has the luster of the color obtained from a peacock's neck and a heated head, is then pure; one should cause it to be drunk.
Those arrows made entirely of iron are proclaimed as *nārācas*;
equipped with five broad feathers, they may occasionally achieve success.
Light arrows propelled by a tube-machine are suited for long-distance shots;
they are considered effective in fortresses and in battles.
One should apply eight positions through distinct movements;
five are declared as *sṛṣṭis* (creations) and five are proclaimed as *vyāyas* (expansions).
In the *ālīḍha* stance, the left foot is placed forward, the right knee is bent,
and likewise, the [left] leg is bent in the *prakartaka* manner.
For a long-distance throw, it is better to aim either to the right or to the front;
the two feet should not be spread wide apart, but kept level at a distance of one cubit.
The special standing position is to be known for piercing the target at its center;
when the fall is even, the two feet are level, steady, and well-knit together.
They know that [posture] to be one where, on an uneven front portion of the ground measuring only a cubit,
the two knees— having their thighs slightly bent— are placed upon the earth.
Taking his stand upon the ground, he assumed the firm-breaking posture (sthānaka),
with his left knee pressed against the earth and his right leg well-bent.
When the left knee is bent upon the ground while the right is not bent,
and it is placed forward, one should know that to be the Garuḍa step.
Having sat down in the well-known lotus posture (padmāsana) according to the proper sequence,
one should here understand the auspiciously characterized standing posture of the archers.
The patākā, guṇamuṣṭi, and likewise the siṃhakarṇa,
as well as the matsarī and the kākatuṇḍī, should be applied in their proper sequence.
Where the long index finger rests at the base of the thumb, that is to be known as the *patākā* (banner) mudrā; the *nālikā* (tube) is used for shooting at a distance.
If the thumb enters between the index and middle fingers, that should be known as the Guṇamuṣṭi; it is used for discharging thick iron arrows (nārāca).
When the tip of the index finger rests auspiciously upon the middle of the thumb,
that is to be known as the "Lion’s Ear" (siṃhakarṇa), used for piercing at a firm target.
When the tip of the index finger is well-placed at the base of the thumb nail,
that is to be known as the *matsarī* [mudrā], for piercing subtle targets.
When the tip of the index finger is placed upon the tip of the thumb,
that is to be known as the *kākatuṇḍī* (crow-beak) mudrā, employed for coarse targets.
The conjunction is said to be threefold—downward, upward, and equal;
indeed, one should apply these three modes according to the sequence in all ritual actions.
When the target is fixed very far away on level ground,
one should make the tip of the bow firm and apply it while aiming upwards.
The Kaiśika style is at the base of the arrow, the Sāttvika at the tip of the arrow;
the Vatsakarṇa is at the ear, and the Bharata should be at the neck.
The five types of arrows are proclaimed as follows:
the *aṃsaka* and the *skandha*, the *vyāya*, the *kaiśika* for various battles, and the *sāttvika* for low targets.
Vatsakarṇa is to be known [as the joint] at Bharata, which is for firm piercing;
and at Dṛḍhabheda and at a distance, one should designate the joint named Skandha.
The objective (lakṣya) is to be known as fourfold:
the stable, the moving, the moving-and-stable, and that which moves both ways; these are the divisions in their respective order.
Having made himself steady and the target likewise steady, the wise man should pierce it in three ways; he is called a "steadfast piercer."
But he who, remaining steady in himself, pierces that which is moving,
is indeed called a "piercer of the moving" (calavedhin) by the Teacher Śiva.
But when the archer, though concentrated on a steady target, moves, then that [target] becomes moving and unmoving; this is declared to be measurable by means of dream.

Where both [the archer and the target] are moving, or where the target is moving while the archer is stationary, that should be known as "dual-moving"; indeed, the practitioner accomplishes it only through great effort.
Through exertion, the target becomes immovable, far-reaching, and capable of piercing many;
through exertion, the fist becomes firm and swift in its execution.
Through exertion, one attains skill in various piercing; through exertion, victory is achieved.
Therefore, a wise person should apply effort in the presence of a teacher.
If a man first performs his labor with the left hand,
the accomplishment of his work will arise very quickly indeed.
When success has been achieved with the left hand, one should thereafter begin with the right;
then one may exert effort with both hands, using iron arrows as well as ordinary shafts.
One should perform the exertion with the left hand alone once the right hand is well-mastered;
likewise in the Viśākha position, as well as in the Vyāya and Kaiśika positions.
When the sun has risen, one should fix the target in the west;
and in the afternoon, the target should be placed in the eastern direction.
One should always perform praiseworthy and obstructive actions toward the north;
one must never aim toward the south, except in the case of battle.
A target within a distance of sixty *khaṇḍas* is proclaimed the superior target;
forty is the middling, and twenty is the inferior.
This has indeed been described regarding arrows; now hear concerning iron shafts (nārācas).
Then, he who practices at the target with forty, sixteen, and forty arrows,
as well as four hundred shafts,
shall become the foremost among archers at sunrise and at sunset.
The middle [size] is with three hundred [units], and the smallest is with two hundred; one should fashion the target according to the measurement of a man, joined with a crescent moon.
One who strikes above the target is the best; one who strikes at the navel is middling;
he who strikes only the feet of the target is the very lowest.
Henceforth, I shall describe the auspicious characteristics of arrows:
those that are too thick, those that are too thin, and those produced from unripe or ripe wood.
One should avoid such an arrow as is crooked or shattered;
rather, one should use an arrow with a full knot, well-ripened, pale-white, and obtained at the proper time.
One should take a hard, round arrow-head produced from an excellent region;
it should be two hand-spans long, excluding the fist, and its thickness should be that of the little finger.
When the moon is waxing, one should then have arrows made;
the feathers of the heron, swan, and hawk, as well as those of fish-eaters, curlews, cuckoos, vultures, and deer— these are auspicious for these [arrows].
One should cause four feathers to be attached to a single arrow;
one should not make a variation in the feathers exceeding the measure of six finger-breadths.
For an arrow of the Śārṅga bow, the feathers should be ten finger-breadths in length.
Four firm, well-fastened, and bound with sinew-threads should be employed;
and arrows are to be known as being of three kinds: female, male, and neuter.
If the woman is stout in the front and the man is stout in the rear,
it should be known as equal, which is praised for the purpose of discerning its characteristics.
The wise know the characteristics of arrows to be as follows: a man [shoots] a long distance, a young woman [shoots] with firm penetration, and a eunuch [shoots] by hitting the mark.
The eighth day, as well as the new moon, the fourteenth day,
and the full moon— these should be avoided for all ritual acts throughout the day.
When the god thunders out of season or when there is foul weather,
they declare it a time unfit for study if the target has been struck by the first arrow.
If, while one is exerting effort, a snake is seen there,
or if the bow breaks during the act of exertion;
O best among the wise, one should not exert effort with a weapon at which the string snaps upon the first discharge of an arrow.
I shall describe the well-known *kriyā-kapālas*, which are accomplished through strenuous effort;
by the mere knowledge of them, success is attained, and not otherwise.
First, having strung the bow, one should then twirl the bowstring;
thereafter, one should assume the proper stance and place the hand upon the arrow.
One should perform the balancing of the bow and ensure steadiness with the left hand; then, having performed the drawing, one should thereafter perform the aiming.
Having drawn [the arrow] from the target with his bow, he should not cause it to pierce the ground;
rather, in battle, they should pay homage to Śiva, Gaṇeśa, and their preceptor.
One should seek the permission of the Guru regarding the drawing of the arrow;
with effort, one should fill the vital breath along with the arrow.
Having drawn [the breath] in with the *kumbhaka* [retention], one should release it with the syllable *huṃ*.
Thus should the practice of exercise be performed by an archer desiring success.
The fist-missile is perfected in six months, and the arrows in a year;
but for him with whom Maheśvara is pleased, the iron shafts (nārāca) are perfected.
One who desires his own success should hold the arrow like a flower, draw the bow like a serpent,
and fix his mind on the target like wealth.
The teachers desire action, the Bhārgavas desire distance;
kings desire vision, while others desire the target.
Since pleasing the people arises from hitting the target even with an inferior arrow,
therefore, hitting the target is praised.
Standing in the Viśākha position, one should perform the equal alignment (sandhāna) with the Gopuccha-mukha-bāṇa, Siṃhakarṇa, and Muṣṭi [mudrās].
In the Kaiśika-vyāya, one should draw [the object] in and then move the crest-lock;
the front and back [hands] should be made equal, with the shoulders level and the hands steady.
One should not blink the eyes, but fix the gaze upon the target;
one should place the target, covered by the fist, at the tip of the arrow.
Having meditated upon [the target] as being held within the grasp of the mind, one should then release the arrow;
that [practice] should be performed upon targets, until the warrior has conquered fatigue regarding the target.
He who, acting with great speed, performs the taking of an arrow from the quiver, as well as its aiming, drawing, and discharge;
Through the power of constant practice, there will be swift accomplishment for him.
Having assumed the *pratyālīḍha* stance, one should perform the downward aim with the fist and the *patākā* hand; this is the "female" method for shooting arrows at long range.
Having performed the *upasthāna* like a frog, one should practice the upward joining (*ūrdhvasandhāna*).
By means of the shoulder-exercise of the *vajra*, and by striking with the fist toward the male organ,
extreme proficiency of the arms and firm penetration are produced.
The needle-mouthed, the fish-tail, and the third, the bee-like—
these three trajectories of arrows are declared by the wise to be excellent.
The path of that arrow becomes like the point of a needle;
its feathered end must be observed, or else it may be one with missing feathers.
When an arrow is drawn by a bow that is too stiff and with a loose grip,
its flight is proclaimed to be like the tail of a fish.
This is indeed called *bhrāmarī* by the wise in the context of laborious work;
for an arrow being discharged does not travel straight without it.
Moving to the left, moving to the right, moving upward, and likewise moving downward—
these four movements are declared to be the causes for the arrow's deviation.
If the fist of the virtues trembles behind the seeker,
while the fist of the bow faces him directly, then there will be movement to the left.
That arrow whose grip is loose and which is devoid of straightness will undoubtedly veer toward the right side.
If the grip on the bow is held too high and the grip on the string is held too low, the released arrow will go above the target;
of this there is no doubt.
In the act of drawing the arrow on the bow, the grip on the bow should be low;
the grip on the string should be high, and then the movement of the arrow will be downward.
When there is a convergence of the eye, the arrow, and the tip [of the arrow],
then the released arrow certainly does not deviate from the target.
Free from defects, devoid of flaws in sound, and released with both fists held level, the arrow pierces even the most solid objects; of this there is no doubt.
Drawn, sharpened, purified, and firmly released—
that arrow does not remain within the bodies of men or of elephants.
He for whom arrows are like blades of grass, whose bow is equal to its stringing,
and whose bowstring is as dear to him as his own life— that archer is the best among archers.
An iron vessel, a leather bag, a water-pot, and a lump of clay—these four;
he who pierces these cannot be harmed even by the arrow of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt.
One should have iron vessels made with a measurement of one and a half finger-breadths;
by piercing them with a single arrow, a man becomes a firm striker.
The arrow of that man who pierces twenty-four shields with a single shaft passes through, having pierced the body of a lordly elephant.
A jar should be pierced while its water is swirling, and likewise a lump of clay on a spinning wheel;
he who pierces these while they are rotating is called a "firm piercer."
One should pierce iron with a crow-beak [awl], leather with a needle-mouthed tool,
and indeed, a lump of clay or a jar with a needle-mouthed tool.
He who knows the arrow-breaker, the whirlpool, the wood-cutter, as well as the dot and the pair, shall be victorious.
Then, having aimed the arrow directly at the target, one should strike it;
having slightly adjusted one's own grip, [one should aim] transversely at the two wooden boards with the shaft.
One should not discharge a transverse arrow at an incoming arrow that is directly facing him;
he who cuts down an arrow already reached by his own arrow is called a "cutter of arrows."
Having tied a horse-hair to a piece of wood and fastened a cowrie shell to it there, [one should proceed].
And he who strikes [the target] while it is being whirled by hand is a true archer.
One should place the weapon in five ways, pure like a bandhūka flower;
he who performs the "elephant-like" (*hāstika*) and "dot" (*binduka*) strokes is called a master of variegated piercing (*citrabhedī*).
The wooden target, pierced at its mark, stands high and far away;
indeed, with its tail raised and mouth facing upward, it has itself presented its back for the arrow.
He who slays with a pair of arrows through the practice of rapid aiming shall be the best among archers, honored by all kings.
One should place a piece of wood, moist and resembling a cow's tail, at the location of the target;
he who pierces it with a razor-sharp arrow is known as a "wood-piercer."
One should place a bell-metal vessel at the location of the target, two cubits away;
one should strike it with sugar-candy until a sound is produced.
Wherever sound is perceived, one should contemplate that [object] there;
through the conjunction of the organs of action, the mind, and the object, one should bring the target to a state of certainty.
Furthermore, one should strike with a saw that has been split by a diamond for the sake of producing sound;
then, with focused attention, the wise man should strike it with an arrow.
This is a difficult task that succeeds only through the good fortune of some rare individual.
Then one should perform the rite of exertion until accomplishment arises;
once exertion has been perfected, during the rainy season, nothing at all should be accepted from the Dhanuṣkara.
In order to avoid forgetting previously practiced weapons,
one should exert effort for two months every year during the autumn season.
When the ninth lunar day of the goddess has arisen in the month of Āśvayuja,
one should worship the Goddess Caṇḍī, the preceptor, the scriptures, and the horses.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins and then honor the young maidens;
one should offer an animal sacrifice to the Goddess accompanied by songs, musical instruments, and auspicious rites.
Protect us with your trident, O Goddess; protect us with your sword, O Ambika;
protect us with the sound of your bell and with the twang of your bowstring.
Protect me in the east, O Caṇḍikā, and protect me in the west; protect me in the south by the whirling of your own trident, and likewise in the north, O Īśvarī.
Whatever gentle forms wander through the three worlds,
and whatever forms are exceedingly terrible— with those, protect us as well as this earth.

Thereupon, for the sake of accomplishing the rites of the weapons, one should master the mantras declared in the Vedas and proclaimed in the Āgamas through the performance of recitation and fire-offerings.
One should accomplish the Brahma, Nārāyaṇa, Śaiva, Aindra, Vāyavya, Vāruṇa,
or Āgneya weapons as bestowed by one's preceptor.
Pervaded by the actions of mind, speech, and body, the weapons of one who has acquired them and is pure burn the person who is unworthy and incapable.
He who understands both the application and the withdrawal of the bow is a true archer;
a wise man should not employ missiles in ordinary tasks.
Having taken the root of the lāṅgalī plant under the constellation Hasta, by means of its application as an ointment,
it instantly robs even a brave man of his pride in battle.
Having taken the root of the Apāmārga plant under the auspicious conjunctions of the Yoga-nakṣatras,
merely by its application as an ointment, all weapons are warded off by heroes.
Adhaḥpuṣpī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, lajjālu, girikarṇikā,
nīlinī, sahadevī, and likewise the leaves of muñja and arka.
On the day of the Sun, the roots of all Viṣṇukrāntā plants should be gathered;
having bound them on the arm or applied them as an ointment to the body, one wards off all weapons.
No fear arises in him from any creatures such as tigers or from spirits and the like; he has no fear of animals, and the eight Mothers abide within his body.
If a muskrat is caught under the Hasta nakṣatra and ground into powder,
by its power a male elephant will certainly come forward to face men.
Having smeared the powder of *chuchundarī* and *śrīphala* upon his body,
and having smelled its fragrance, even an elephant in extreme rut will abandon its intoxication.
When the root of the *pūga* tree has been uprooted under the asterism Puṣya and placed in the mouth by the sun,
the bodies of men do not burst open even at the edge of a sharp sword in battle.
The root of gambhārī, which has come directly from the topmost part of the tree,
wards off a flood of weapons when it is extracted there according to the ritual on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya constellation.
The matted locks of Śubhrā, Śarapuṅkhā, and likewise Nīlī—
whether situated on the arm, the head, or the face— are warders-off of weapons.
It destroys fear of spirits, snakes, and thieves when taken during the conjunction of Puṣya and the Sun.
First, the ritual bath is performed; one should be clothed in white garments.
Having also worshipped the weapons, one should then recite the protective mantra;
[one should likewise honor] the commander-in-chief, the elephant-riders, and the horse-riders from all sides.
He should cause the principal officers and others as well to be clothed with wealth and garments;
having first placed the charioteer upon the chariot, he should then prepare himself.
One should fill the quiver with four hundred arrows,
as well as a conch, a discus, a mace, a spear, a mallet, and likewise an iron club.
One should station iron arrows, axes, spears, sharp-edged spears, and other weapons at the positions for men, infantry, and elephants; then one should personally enter the battle.
With a single quiver fastened at his waist and wielding a sword, a spear, and a bow,
he then [uttered] the names of Arjuna preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
Then he should mutter [the mantra] and set out, accompanied by a fourfold army.
Auspicious is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; auspicious is he whose banner bears Garuḍa;
auspicious is the lotus-eyed one; Hari is the abode of all auspiciousness.
Blessed are they, victorious are they; how could there be defeat for those in whose hearts dwells Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus?
Arjuna, Phalguna, Jishnu, Kirīṭin, Śvetavāhana, Bībhatsu, Vijaya, Kṛṣṇa, Savyasācin, and Dhanañjaya.
A self-controlled person should thus call to mind the names of Arjuna.
Two thousand [squares] are considered an *akṣauhiṇī* by those who possess the divine power of the gods and the eyes of the moon;
and an *akṣauhiṇī* is also prescribed as the number of chariots for those wearing armor.
Those who know the principles of calculation and enumeration say there are twenty-one thousand,
eight hundred and seventy, O King.
One should specify this very same measurement for the elephants:
sixty-five thousand, six hundred, and ten more.
This very same well-ascertained measure applies to the horses;
it should be known that there are one hundred thousand foot soldiers and likewise nine thousand.
There were three hundred and fifty brave warriors bearing weapons,
as well as sixty-five thousand horses and hundreds more.
Those people who know the true nature of numbers sing of the tenfold increases.
A great akṣauhiṇī is said to consist of ten million chariots.
And thirty-seven hundred thousand verses are sung by those who know the truth,
as well as twelve thousand and four hundred.
In that same manner, ninety elephants are said to be required;
likewise, horses numbering four crores and eleven lakhs are prescribed.
Thirty-seven thousand, four hundred,
and seven are the number by which the foot soldiers are said to be reckoned.
Sixty million, eighty lakhs,
five hundred and sixty-two thousand, as well as four hundred.
Chariots should be placed at the front, elephants at the rear, and infantry behind them;
horses should be stationed on both flanks—this is remembered as the prescribed method for calculating the array of troops.
He thus arranges the battle formations: the half-moon, the moon, the wagon, the sea-monster, the lotus, the row, and the cluster.
Those princes, vassals, trusted ones,
and classes of servants who act for one's welfare must always be protected with great effort.
In whatever battle a man is the leader, he must indeed be protected with every effort;
for when he is destroyed, it is said that all beings—and indeed all the warriors—become powerless.
If you rely upon one who is the very essence of battle and is learned in the treatises,
then this circle of shaven heads is merely a useless army for your own prosperity.
Even five hundred heroes can seize a great army;
or else, only five, six, or seven followers may achieve victory.
Kings whose souls are purified by the mastery of the bow, though weak in speech,
and warriors with hair turned gray at the temples, proclaim their victory in battle.
Those warriors who are mutually devoted, who wield the Śārṅga bow,
and who are skilled in battle while mounted on chariots, conquer their enemies in war.
A single coward may cause a great army to break;
once it has broken, even the bravest warriors follow suit and flee.
And because it is so difficult to restrain, a complete and vast army might terrify even the skilled, just as a great torrent of water does.
Even when the armies are broken and fleeing,
he who turns back at every step obtains the inexhaustible fruit of the horse sacrifice.
There are these two persons in the world who pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle.
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains an imperishable world, provided he does not utter words of dejection.
One should not strike one who is unconscious, nor one who is incapacitated, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who is fighting another, nor one who is fleeing, nor one who has sought refuge.
Even one who is fleeing in fear must not be slain by a stronger person;
for such a person may sometimes display courage once they have forgotten their refuge.
Having mustered a great fourfold army, the lord of the earth,
having arrayed it, should station his heroic warriors against the enemy with a desire for victory.
Whether the army be small or large, this is the certainty:
the joy of the host of warriors is said to be the sign of victory.
When the winds blow in this manner and the birds fly toward the south,
and when all the jackals follow him, victory belongs to that man in battle.
It should be considered incomplete until it is indeed fulfilled; only through fulfillment is success attained.
Therefore, one must exercise fortitude and destroy the enemy host.
While alive there is prosperity, and upon death there is heaven and fame upon the earth;
therefore, one should maintain fortitude and strike down the enemy's army.
Thus ends the Dhanurveda, as proclaimed by the venerable Sadāśiva.
